questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A microscopic specimen in the figure has chlorophyll a and b and stores starch within a chloroplast. Which algal group is most consistent with these linked traits?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Chlorophyceae.
Why: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) have chlorophyll a and b, the same pigments as land plants, and store food as starch. The starch is often laid down around pyrenoids inside the chloroplast.
Why not the others: (B) Brown algae have chlorophyll a and c and fucoxanthin, and store laminarin and mannitol. (C) Red algae have chlorophyll a and d and phycoerythrin, and store floridean starch. (D) Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes and have no chloroplasts.
Key point: Green: a, b, starch. Brown: a, c, laminarin. Red: a, d, floridean starch.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: The flower diagram shows a superior ovary with sepals, petals and stamens attached below it. Which position is represented?
options: D) Inferior ovary with epigynous insertion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Hypogynous.
Why: The position of a flower is named from where the other parts are attached relative to the ovary. When the ovary sits highest and the sepals, petals and stamens arise below it, the flower is hypogynous and the ovary is superior, as in mustard and brinjal.
Why not the others: (A) In an epigynous flower the other parts arise above the ovary, which is inferior. (C) In a perigynous flower the parts arise from the rim of a cup at the same level as the ovary; the ovary is half-inferior. (D) describes the epigynous condition again.
Key point: Hypogynous: superior ovary. Epigynous: inferior ovary.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A eukaryotic messenger RNA leaves the nucleus and is translated into a secreted protein. Where does translation begin and where does elongation proceed after the signal peptide is recognised?
options: C) Cytosolic ribosome, then ribosome associated with rough ER
D) Golgi lumen, then plasma membrane
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cytosolic ribosome, then ribosome associated with rough ER.
Why: All protein synthesis starts on ribosomes free in the cytosol. For a protein that will be secreted, the first part of the chain is a signal sequence. Once it is recognised, the ribosome attaches to the membrane of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the growing chain passes into the ER lumen. From there the protein goes to the Golgi body and is released.
Why not the others: (A) No translation takes place inside the nucleus, and lysosomes digest material. (B) Mitochondria make only a few of their own proteins. (D) The Golgi body modifies and packs proteins made elsewhere; it has no ribosomes.
Key point: Secretory proteins: rough ER → Golgi → vesicle → outside.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the Calvin cycle, three CO₂ molecules are fixed. How many molecules of the three-carbon triose phosphate leave the cycle as the net carbohydrate product while the rest regenerate RuBP?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) One.
Given: 3 CO₂ fixed; each CO₂ joins one RuBP (5 C) to give two molecules of 3-PGA (3 C).
Formula/Principle: Carbon atoms are conserved in the cycle.
Step 1: 3 CO₂ + 3 RuBP → 6 molecules of 3-PGA → 6 triose phosphate (18 C).
Step 2: Regenerating 3 RuBP needs 3 × 5 = 15 C, that is, 5 triose phosphate.
Step 3: Triose phosphate left over = 6 − 5 = 1 (3 C, equal to the 3 C that entered as CO₂).
Why: The cycle must rebuild as much RuBP as it used, or it would stop. Only the carbon that came in as CO₂ can leave as product. Six turns, fixing six CO₂, are needed for one glucose.
Why not the others: (A) Three would remove 9 C when only 3 C entered. (B) Two would remove 6 C. (C) Six is the total number of triose phosphates formed, before regeneration.
Key point: 3 CO₂ in → 1 triose phosphate out; 5 of every 6 regenerate RuBP.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A contracting sarcomere shortens while thin and thick filaments keep their own lengths. Which pair of band changes is expected?
options: A) I band narrows, A band remains approximately constant
B) A band narrows, I band remains constant
C) Both bands narrow in proportion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) I band narrows, A band remains approximately constant.
Why: The A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, which do not change. The I band is the part of the thin filaments not overlapped by thick filaments. In contraction the thin filaments slide inward over the thick ones; the overlap increases, so the I band and the H zone become narrower and the Z lines move closer.
Why not the others: (B) The A band cannot narrow, because the thick filaments keep their length. (C) Only the I band narrows. (D) The sarcomere shortens, so something must change.
Key point: Sliding filaments: I band and H zone shorten, A band constant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Cells of the pollen grain at shedding
questions.question: In most angiosperms the pollen grain is shed at the two-celled stage. Which two cells does it contain?
options: B) A large vegetative cell and a small generative cell
C) An egg cell and a synergid
D) A microspore mother cell and a tapetal cell
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A large vegetative cell and a small generative cell.
Why: The microspore divides once by mitosis into two unequal cells. The larger vegetative cell has a large irregular nucleus and plenty of stored food; it later forms the pollen tube. The small, spindle-shaped generative cell floats in its cytoplasm and divides to give the two male gametes, usually after pollination.
Why not the others: (A) The two male gametes are formed later, by division of the generative cell. (C) The egg and synergids belong to the embryo sac, the female gametophyte. (D) The microspore mother cell and tapetum are parts of the anther, not of the pollen grain.
Key point: Pollen at shedding: vegetative cell + generative cell (2-celled in over 60% of angiosperms).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Role of DNA ligase in replication
questions.question: A mutant bacterium has no working DNA ligase, but all its other replication enzymes are normal. What is expected to build up during DNA replication?
options: A) Unwound parental strands with no new DNA at all
B) RNA copies of both strands
C) Short unjoined DNA fragments made on the lagging-strand template
D) Double-length chromosomes joined end to end
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Short unjoined DNA fragments made on the lagging-strand template.
Why: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5′ → 3′ direction. One new strand is therefore made continuously, and the other is made as short pieces, the Okazaki fragments. DNA ligase joins these pieces into one strand. Without ligase the pieces are still made but stay separate.
Why not the others: (A) Unwinding and synthesis are carried out by helicase and DNA polymerase, which are normal. (B) Making RNA from DNA is transcription, not replication. (D) Ligase joins fragments within a strand; its absence does not join chromosomes together.
Key point: Lagging strand: discontinuous fragments, sealed by DNA ligase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Helper-B-cell cooperation with a downstream bypass
questions.question: Two purified immune-cell populations are tested with the same antigen and all other culture conditions held fixed. B cells alone make little specific antibody; helper T cells alone make none; the combined culture makes much more. Preventing helper-cell signalling in the combined culture reduces antibody production, while supplying ready-made antibody still neutralises the antigen. Which inference is best supported?
options: A) Helper T cells themselves are the only antibody-secreting cells
B) The neutralising antibody can be produced without any B-cell lineage
C) The blocking treatment necessarily destroys antigen
D) Helper T cells promote the B-cell antibody response, while ready-made antibody acts downstream of that cooperation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Helper T cells promote the B-cell antibody response, while ready-made antibody acts downstream of that cooperation.
Why: B cells are the cells that make antibody, but they respond weakly on their own. Helper T cells make no antibody; they send signals that activate B cells. So the two together give a strong response, and blocking the helper signal weakens it. Antibody that has already been made binds antigen directly and needs no further help.
Why not the others: (A) Helper T cells alone made no antibody. (B) Antibodies come only from B cells and the plasma cells derived from them. (C) The block lowers antibody production; nothing shows that it destroys the antigen.
Key point: Helper T cells help; B cells (plasma cells) secrete antibody.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A linear double-stranded DNA target is shown with top strand 5′ at left and 3′ at right. Which primer orientation permits amplification of the interval between the two inward-facing sites?
options: A) Left forward primer extends right; right reverse primer extends left
D) Both primers anneal with 3′ ends pointing outward
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Left forward primer extends right; right reverse primer extends left.
Why: DNA polymerase extends a primer from its 3′ end. For the stretch between the primers to be copied, each primer must bind to a different strand with its 3′ end pointing towards the other primer. The left primer is then extended to the right and the right primer to the left, and after each cycle the amount of this stretch doubles.
Why not the others: (B) If both extend to the right, only one strand is copied and there is no doubling. (C) The same is true if both extend to the left. (D) With the 3′ ends pointing outward, synthesis runs away from the target.
Key point: PCR primers face each other, 3′ ends inward.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Change in population size from births, deaths and migration
questions.question: A population has 100 individuals. During one year there are 30 births and 20 deaths; 10 individuals immigrate and 5 emigrate. What is the population size at the end of the year?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 115.
Given: N₀ = 100; births B = 30; deaths D = 20; immigration I = 10; emigration E = 5.
Formula/Principle: N₁ = N₀ + (B + I) − (D + E).
Step 1: Additions = 30 + 10 = 40.
Step 2: Losses = 20 + 5 = 25.
Step 3: N₁ = 100 + 40 − 25 = 115.
Why: Natality and immigration add to a population; mortality and emigration take away from it. The change in size is the difference between the two totals.
Why not the others: (A) 105 leaves out the 10 immigrants. (C) 125 adds the emigrants and subtracts nothing for them. (D) 165 adds all four numbers.
Key point: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)].

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An mRNA codon reads 5′-AUG-3′. What is the anticodon of the tRNA that pairs with it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3′-UAC-5′.
Why: The anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary bases, A with U and G with C, and the two strands run in opposite directions. Under 5′-A-U-G-3′ the pairing bases are U, A and C, read 3′ to 5′. This is the anticodon of the initiator tRNA, which carries methionine.
Why not the others: (A) repeats the codon; identical bases do not pair. (B) contains thymine, which does not occur in a tRNA anticodon in this pairing. (D) has the same bases as the codon, simply relabelled.
Key point: Codon 5′→3′ pairs with anticodon 3′→5′; RNA uses U, not T.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An mRNA reading frame begins AUG–GAA–UAA. If translation begins at the first AUG, how many amino acids are incorporated before termination?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Two.
Why: Reading starts at AUG, which codes for methionine. The next codon, GAA, codes for glutamic acid. The third codon, UAA, is a stop codon: no tRNA matches it, and a release factor ends the chain. Two amino acids have been joined.
Why not the others: (A) One would mean stopping after AUG. (B) Three treats UAA as coding for an amino acid. (C) There are only three codons in all.
Key point: Stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA code for no amino acid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two patients have similarly low circulating thyroid hormone. Patient P has high TSH; patient Q has low TSH. Which distinction is most consistent with intact negative feedback in P and impaired pituitary drive in Q?
options: A) Neither can have thyroid disease
B) P has pituitary failure, Q has primary thyroid failure
C) Both necessarily have iodine excess
D) P has primary thyroid failure, Q may have secondary pituitary failure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P has primary thyroid failure, Q may have secondary pituitary failure.
Why: Thyroid hormone normally holds back the release of TSH from the pituitary. In P the hormone is low and TSH is high: the pituitary is responding correctly and trying to drive the thyroid, so the fault lies in the thyroid. In Q the hormone is low, yet TSH is also low: the pituitary is not responding, so the thyroid is under-stimulated.
Why not the others: (A) Both have low thyroid hormone, which is abnormal. (B) has the two the wrong way round. (C) Nothing in the data points to iodine, and the two patterns differ.
Key point: Low hormone with high TSH: gland fault. Low hormone with low TSH: pituitary fault.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: DNA content through the cell cycle and meiosis
questions.question: A diploid cell of an animal has 20 pg of DNA in the G₁ phase. How much DNA does the cell have in G₂, and how much does each gamete formed from it by meiosis have?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 40 pg; 10 pg.
Given: G₁ (2C) = 20 pg.
Formula/Principle: S phase doubles the DNA; each of the two meiotic divisions halves it.
Step 1: G₂ = 2 × 20 = 40 pg (4C).
Step 2: After meiosis I each cell has 40 ÷ 2 = 20 pg (2C).
Step 3: After meiosis II each gamete has 20 ÷ 2 = 10 pg (1C).
Why: DNA is replicated once, in S phase, but the nucleus divides twice in meiosis. A gamete therefore has half the DNA of a G₁ cell, and a quarter of that of a G₂ cell.
Why not the others: (A) 20 pg in G₂ ignores replication. (C) 20 pg is the content after meiosis I, not of a gamete. (D) ignores replication and halves twice.
Key point: 2C → 4C (S phase) → 2C (meiosis I) → 1C (meiosis II).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A DNA digest gel has a 900 bp band in lane X and 600 bp plus 300 bp bands in lane Y; full sample DNA lengths are 900 bp. Which statement follows from band positions alone?
options: A) Lane Y contains twice as much DNA as lane X
B) Lane X is necessarily heterozygous
C) Lane Y DNA was cut at one internal position, while X was not cut at that site
D) The 600 bp fragment must fluoresce twice as brightly as the 300 bp band
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lane Y DNA was cut at one internal position, while X was not cut at that site.
Why: In a gel, smaller fragments travel farther. Lane X has one band at the full length, 900 bp, so that DNA was not cut. Lane Y has two bands whose sizes add up to the full length, 600 + 300 = 900 bp, so that DNA was cut once, 300 bp from one end.
Why not the others: (A) Band position shows size, not the amount of DNA. (B) A heterozygote would show all three bands: 900, 600 and 300 bp. (D) Brightness is not given, and in any case the two fragments are present in equal numbers.
Key point: Fragment sizes add up to the size of the uncut DNA.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The structures show NH₃ and NF₃ with three bonds and one lone pair on central nitrogen. Which has the larger H–N–H or F–N–F bond angle, respectively?
options: A) NH₃, because N–H bond pairs stay nearer N than N–F bond pairs
B) NF₃, because F is larger than H
C) Equal, because both have four domains
D) NF₃, because lone pairs vanish in polar bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) NH₃, because N–H bond pairs stay nearer N than N–F bond pairs.
Why: Both molecules are pyramidal with one lone pair. In NH₃ nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the bonding pairs lie close to nitrogen and repel one another strongly; the angle is about 107°. In NF₃ fluorine pulls the bonding pairs away from nitrogen, so they repel less and the lone pair squeezes them closer; the angle is about 102°.
Why not the others: (B) The size of fluorine is not the deciding factor, and the angle in NF₃ is in fact smaller. (C) The same number of domains does not mean the same angle. (D) The lone pair on nitrogen is present in both molecules.
Key point: Bond pairs nearer the central atom repel more: larger angle.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Coordination number and oxidation state with a bidentate ligand
questions.question: In the complex ion [Co(en)₃]³⁺, where en is ethane-1,2-diamine, what are the coordination number and the oxidation state of cobalt?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6 and +3.
Why: Ethane-1,2-diamine is a bidentate ligand: each molecule binds through its two nitrogen atoms. Three such ligands give 3 × 2 = 6 Co–N bonds, so the coordination number is 6. The ligand is neutral, so the charge on the ion, +3, is the oxidation state of cobalt.
Why not the others: (A) 3 is the number of ligands, not of donor atoms. (C) An oxidation state of 0 would leave the complex with no charge. (D) confuses the two numbers.
Key point: Coordination number = number of donor atoms bonded, not number of ligands.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Infer an unpaired-electron count from a magnetic moment
questions.question: An ion's measured spin-only magnetic moment is \(\sqrt{24}\) Bohr magnetons. How many unpaired electrons does the spin-only model assign, and what is the ratio of that number to the count for a \(\sqrt3\)-BM ion?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 and 4.
Given: \(\mu_1=\sqrt{24}\ \mathrm{BM}\); \(\mu_2=\sqrt3\ \mathrm{BM}\).
Formula/Principle: Spin-only formula \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \mathrm{BM}\), n = number of unpaired electrons.
Step 1: \(n(n+2)=24\Rightarrow n^2+2n-24=0\Rightarrow(n-4)(n+6)=0\Rightarrow n=4\).
Step 2: \(n(n+2)=3\Rightarrow(n-1)(n+3)=0\Rightarrow n=1\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{n_1}{n_2}=\frac41=4\]
Why: The magnetic moment of first-row transition-metal ions comes almost entirely from electron spin, so it depends only on the number of unpaired electrons. The values √3, √8, √15, √24 and √35 correspond to 1 to 5 unpaired electrons.
Why not the others: (A) n = 2 gives √8. (B) n = 3 gives √15. (D) n = 6 gives √48.
Key point: \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Two electrons are proposed in the same atom with identical (n,l,m_l,m_s) quantum numbers. Which rule rules this out even if the orbital energies are equal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Pauli exclusion principle.
Why: The Pauli principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. Two electrons in one orbital share n, l and m_l, so they must differ in spin: one +½ and one −½. This is why an orbital holds at most two electrons.
Why not the others: (A) Hund's rule deals with how electrons spread over orbitals of equal energy. (B) The aufbau principle gives the order in which orbitals are filled. (C) The uncertainty principle limits how well position and momentum can be known together.
Key point: One orbital: at most two electrons, with opposite spins.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: Among Be, B, N and O in the second period, which paired first-ionisation-energy comparisons are both correct, and what orbital effects explain them?
options: A) Be>B due to starting a 2p electron in B; N>O because paired 2p electrons in O repel
B) B>Be due to greater nuclear charge; O>N due to greater nuclear charge
C) Be>B because Be has a filled 2p shell; N>O because N has no p electrons
D) B>Be because B is more metallic; N>O because O has a half-filled p shell
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Be>B due to starting a 2p electron in B; N>O because paired 2p electrons in O repel.
Why: Ionisation enthalpy generally rises across a period, with two dips. Boron's outermost electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and better shielded than the 2s electrons of beryllium, so it is removed more easily. Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p subshell, 2p³; in oxygen, 2p⁴, the fourth electron must pair up, and the extra repulsion makes it easier to remove.
Why not the others: (B) Nuclear charge alone would predict the opposite order, which is not what is observed. (C) Beryllium has no 2p electrons at all, and nitrogen has three. (D) Oxygen is 2p⁴; the half-filled subshell belongs to nitrogen.
Key point: Period 2: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Unknown initial gas composition from a cooled residual
questions.question: A hydrogen–oxygen gas mixture has volume 30.0 mL. After complete reaction and cooling until all product water condenses, 5.0 mL oxygen remains. All gas volumes are compared at the same temperature and pressure; neither initial gas contains water. What was the initial hydrogen volume?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(50/3\) mL.
Given: Total 30.0 mL of \(\ce{H2}\) + \(\ce{O2}\); 5.0 mL \(\ce{O2}\) left; water condensed.
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}\); at the same T and p, volumes of gases are in the ratio of moles.
Step 1: Volume that reacted \(=30.0-5.0=25.0\ \mathrm{mL}\).
Step 2: The reacting gases are in the ratio \(\ce{H2}:\ce{O2}=2:1\).
Worked derivation: \[V(\ce{H2})=\frac23\times25.0=\frac{50}{3}\ \mathrm{mL}=16.7\ \mathrm{mL}\]
Why: Oxygen is left over, so all the hydrogen was used. The 25 mL that disappeared was two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen. A check: oxygen at the start = 25/3 + 5 = 13.3 mL, and 16.7 + 13.3 = 30.0 mL.
Why not the others: (A) 25.0 mL is the whole volume that reacted, hydrogen and oxygen together. (C) 20.0 mL would use 10 mL of oxygen and leave none. (D) 10.0 mL would use 5 mL of oxygen and leave 15 mL.
Key point: Subtract the residue first, then split the rest in the ratio of the equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which acid is stronger in water, CH₃COOH or ClCH₂COOH, and why?
options: A) CH₃COOH because methyl withdraws electrons
B) Equal because both are carboxylic acids
C) ClCH₂COOH because chlorine withdraws electron density inductively and stabilises its conjugate base
D) ClCH₂COOH because it has more resonance structures
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ClCH₂COOH because chlorine withdraws electron density inductively and stabilises its conjugate base.
Why: An acid is stronger when its conjugate base is more stable. Chlorine is electronegative and pulls electrons along the σ bonds (−I effect). This spreads the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilises it. pK_a falls from 4.76 for ethanoic acid to 2.86 for chloroethanoic acid.
Why not the others: (A) A methyl group releases electrons, which makes the anion less stable. (B) Substituents change acid strength considerably. (D) Both carboxylate ions have the same two resonance structures; the difference is inductive.
Key point: Electron-withdrawing groups increase acid strength.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reactivity of aldehydes and ketones in nucleophilic addition
questions.question: Why is ethanal more reactive than propanone towards nucleophilic addition?
options: A) Ethanal has no carbonyl group
B) Propanone has a more positive carbonyl carbon
C) Ethanal has two alkyl groups that push the nucleophile towards the carbon
D) Propanone has two alkyl groups, which hinder the attack and reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Propanone has two alkyl groups, which hinder the attack and reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
Why: Two effects work in the same direction. Sterically, the two methyl groups of a ketone crowd the carbonyl carbon more than the one alkyl group and one hydrogen of an aldehyde. Electronically, alkyl groups release electrons and lower the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so it attracts a nucleophile less.
Why not the others: (A) Ethanal does have a carbonyl group. (B) The carbonyl carbon of propanone is less positive, not more. (C) Ethanal has only one alkyl group, and alkyl groups do not push a nucleophile towards the carbon.
Key point: Reactivity to nucleophilic addition: HCHO > RCHO > RCOR.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A liquid gives H₂ with sodium metal but no CO₂ with aqueous NaHCO₃. It is soluble in water and has no carbonyl peak. Which class is best supported?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Alcohol.
Why: Sodium reacts with any compound that has an O–H bond and gives hydrogen. Sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts only with acids stronger than carbonic acid, such as carboxylic acids. An alcohol is far too weak an acid to release CO₂. Solubility in water and the absence of a carbonyl group agree with a small alcohol.
Why not the others: (B) A carboxylic acid would give CO₂ with NaHCO₃ and has a carbonyl group. (C) An aldehyde has a carbonyl group and gives no hydrogen with sodium. (D) A hydrocarbon does not react with sodium and does not dissolve in water.
Key point: Na: any –OH. NaHCO₃: only –COOH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Directing-group strategy followed by diazonium replacement
questions.question: Starting with benzene, which order of operations gives predominantly 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene? Use ordinary electrophilic directing effects, selective nitro-group reduction, and Sandmeyer replacement of an aryl diazonium group by Cl.
options: A) Brominate; nitrate; reduce NO₂; diazotise then CuCl
B) Nitrate; brominate; reduce NO₂; diazotise at 0–5°C then CuCl
C) Nitrate; reduce NO₂; brominate directly with bromine water; diazotise then CuCl
D) Chlorinate; brominate; nitrate; reduce NO₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Nitrate; brominate; reduce NO₂; diazotise at 0–5°C then CuCl.
Why: The target has Br and Cl meta to each other, but both halogens direct ortho and para. A meta-directing group must therefore be put on first. Nitration gives nitrobenzene; the nitro group sends bromine to the meta position. Reducing the nitro group gives 3-bromoaniline, and diazotisation followed by CuCl (Sandmeyer reaction) replaces the amino group by chlorine at the same carbon.
Why not the others: (A) Bromine first directs the nitro group ortho and para, so the final product is the 1,2 or 1,4 isomer. (C) Aniline is so strongly activated that bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. (D) Chlorine directs bromine ortho and para, and the nitro group is never changed into anything useful.
Key point: Choose the order of steps from the directing effect of the group already on the ring.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch but not cellulose. What is the structural difference between them?
options: A) Starch contains fructose units as well
B) Cellulose is a polymer of amino acids
C) Starch has α-glucose units joined by α-glycosidic links; cellulose has β-glucose units joined by β-1,4 links
D) Cellulose is branched and starch is never branched
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Starch has α-glucose units joined by α-glycosidic links; cellulose has β-glucose units joined by β-1,4 links.
Why: Starch is made of amylose (α-1,4 links) and amylopectin (α-1,4 links with α-1,6 branches). Cellulose is a straight chain of β-D-glucose joined by β-1,4 links. Human digestive enzymes such as amylase fit and break α-links only, so cellulose passes through undigested.
Why not the others: (A) Starch gives only glucose on hydrolysis. (B) Cellulose is a carbohydrate, not a protein. (D) It is the other way round: cellulose is unbranched, and the amylopectin of starch is branched.
Key point: Starch: α-links. Cellulose: β-links.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Nonideal vapour pressure and mixing energetics
questions.question: A binary liquid mixture has vapour pressure above its Raoult-law ideal value at intermediate composition. Which pair of mixing tendencies is most consistent with the usual positive-deviation model?
options: A) Stronger unlike attractions; heat released
B) Stronger unlike attractions; heat absorbed
C) Weaker unlike attractions; heat released
D) Weaker unlike attractions; heat absorbed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Weaker unlike attractions; heat absorbed.
Why: A vapour pressure above the Raoult's-law value means that molecules escape more easily from the mixture than from the pure liquids. That happens when A–B attractions are weaker than the A–A and B–B attractions they replace. Replacing stronger attractions by weaker ones needs energy, so heat is absorbed on mixing (Δ_mixH > 0), and the volume usually increases. Ethanol with acetone is an example.
Why not the others: (A) Stronger unlike attractions with heat released describe negative deviation. (B) Stronger attractions would release heat, not absorb it. (C) Weaker attractions cannot release heat.
Key point: Positive deviation: A–B weaker, ΔH > 0, ΔV > 0.
questions.syllabus_anchor: Solutions: positive deviation from Raoult law

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: What happens at the electrodes of a lead storage battery while it is delivering current (discharging)?
options: A) Both the Pb anode and the PbO₂ cathode are converted to PbSO₄, and sulfuric acid is used up
B) Lead is deposited on both electrodes and the acid becomes more concentrated
C) Only the anode reacts; the cathode is inert
D) Hydrogen and oxygen are given off and no solid forms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both the Pb anode and the PbO₂ cathode are converted to PbSO₄, and sulfuric acid is used up.
Why: At the anode: Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻. At the cathode: PbO₂ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Overall: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulfuric acid is consumed and water is formed, so the density of the acid falls; this is used to test the state of charge. Charging reverses the reactions.
Why not the others: (B) Lead is not deposited, and the acid becomes more dilute. (C) Both electrodes take part. (D) Gases are not the products of discharge; solid PbSO₄ forms on both plates.
Key point: Discharge: Pb and PbO₂ → PbSO₄; acid is consumed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A first-order reaction has half-life 20 min. After 60 min, what fraction of initial reactant remains?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/8.
Given: First order; \(t_{1/2}=20\ \mathrm{min}\); \(t=60\ \mathrm{min}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{[A]}{[A]_0}=\left(\dfrac12\right)^{t/t_{1/2}}\).
Step 1: Number of half-lives \(=60/20=3\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{[A]}{[A]_0}=\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac18\]
Why: For a first-order reaction the half-life is constant, whatever the concentration. The amount therefore halves in each 20 minutes: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8.
Why not the others: (A) 1/4 is the fraction after two half-lives. (B) 1/32 is after five. (C) 1/16 is after four.
Key point: Fraction left after n half-lives = (1/2)ⁿ.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the diagram gives an equilibrium mixture with pNO2=2 atm and pN2O4=1 atm, then NO₂ pressure is instantaneously increased to 4 atm at constant T before reaction. Relative to the old equilibrium, which way does reaction initially proceed?
options: A) Right because NO₂ was added
B) No shift because T is unchanged
C) Left because Qp rises from 4 to 16
D) Right because the product pressure is squared
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Left because Qp rises from 4 to 16.
Given: \(\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}\); at equilibrium \(p_{\ce{NO2}}=2\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(p_{\ce{N2O4}}=1\ \mathrm{atm}\); then \(p_{\ce{NO2}}=4\ \mathrm{atm}\).
Formula/Principle: \(Q_p=\dfrac{p_{\ce{NO2}}^2}{p_{\ce{N2O4}}}\); if \(Q_p>K_p\) the reaction goes backward.
Step 1: \(K_p=\dfrac{2^2}{1}=4\).
Step 2: After the addition, \(Q_p=\dfrac{4^2}{1}=16\).
Worked derivation: \[Q_p=16>K_p=4\Rightarrow\text{net reaction to the left}\]
Why: K_p stays the same because the temperature has not changed. The mixture now has too much product for equilibrium, so NO₂ combines to form N₂O₄ until Q_p falls back to 4. This agrees with Le Chatelier's principle.
Why not the others: (A) Adding a product drives the reaction backward, not forward. (B) A constant temperature keeps K_p fixed, but Q_p has changed. (D) Squaring the product pressure raises Q_p, which favours the reverse reaction.
Key point: Q > K: backward. Q < K: forward.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A hyperbola has equation x²/9−y²/16=1. What is the acute angle θ that either asymptote makes with the positive x-axis, through tan θ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4/3.
Given: \(\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1\Rightarrow a=3,\ b=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{asymptotes}:\ y=\pm\dfrac bax\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=0\Rightarrow y=\pm\dfrac43x\)
Worked derivation: \[\tan\theta=\frac ba=\frac43\]
Check: \[x\to\infty:\ y=\frac43\sqrt{x^2-9}\to\frac43x\]
Why: \(\text{slope}=\tan(\text{angle with the }x\text{-axis})\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac ab=\dfrac34\); (C) \(\dfrac bc=\dfrac45=\sin\theta\); (D) \(\dfrac cb=\dfrac54\).
Key point: \(\text{asymptotes of }\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1:\ y=\pm\dfrac bax\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The line \(3x+4y=12\) meets the axes at A and B. A circle has AB as a diameter. What is the tangent to this circle at the origin?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(4x+3y=0\).
Given: \(3x+4y=12\Rightarrow A=(4,0),\ B=(0,3);\quad AB\ \text{a diameter}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{tangent}\perp\text{radius at the point of contact}\)
Step 1: \(\text{centre}=\left(2,\tfrac32\right),\quad r=\tfrac12\sqrt{16+9}=\tfrac52\)
Step 2: \(|OC|=\sqrt{4+\tfrac94}=\tfrac52=r\Rightarrow O\ \text{lies on the circle}\)
Step 3: \(\text{radius }OC\ \text{has direction}\ \left(2,\tfrac32\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[2x+\tfrac32y=0\Rightarrow4x+3y=0\]
Check: \[\text{distance from }\left(2,\tfrac32\right)\text{ to }4x+3y=0:\ \frac{8+4.5}{5}=\frac52=r\]
Why: \(\angle AOB=90^\circ\Rightarrow O\ \text{on the circle with diameter }AB\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3x+4y=0\ \parallel AB\); (C) \(4x-3y=0:\ \dfrac{|8-4.5|}{5}=0.7\ne\dfrac52\); (D) \(x+y=0:\ \dfrac{3.5}{\sqrt2}\ne\dfrac52\).
Key point: \(\text{tangent at }P:\ (\mathbf r-\mathbf P)\cdot(\mathbf P-\mathbf C)=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=ax² for x≤1 and f(x)=bx+c for x>1. If f is differentiable at x=1 and f(2)=5, what is c?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −5/3.
Given: \(f(x)=ax^2\ (x\le1),\quad f(x)=bx+c\ (x>1),\quad f(2)=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{continuity}:\ a=b+c;\quad\text{equal derivatives}:\ 2a=b\)
Step 1: \(a=\dfrac b2\Rightarrow\dfrac b2=b+c\Rightarrow c=-\dfrac b2\)
Step 2: \(f(2)=2b+c=2b-\dfrac b2=\dfrac{3b}{2}=5\Rightarrow b=\dfrac{10}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[c=-\frac b2=-\frac53\]
Check: \[a=\tfrac53:\ f(1)=\tfrac53=\tfrac{10}{3}-\tfrac53;\quad f'(1^-)=\tfrac{10}{3}=f'(1^+)\]
Why: \(\text{differentiable}\Rightarrow\text{continuous and equal one-sided derivatives}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(c=-1:\ b=3,\ a=\tfrac32,\ a\ne b+c\); (B) \(c=1:\ b=2,\ a=1\ne3\); (D) \(c=5:\ b=0,\ a=0\ne5\).
Key point: \(\text{two conditions at the junction, one from the given value}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^1xe^x\,dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1xe^x\,dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du,\quad u=x,\ dv=e^x\,dx\)
Step 1: \(I=\left[xe^x\right]_0^1-\displaystyle\int_0^1e^x\,dx\)
Step 2: \(I=e-(e-1)\)
Worked derivation: \[I=1\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[(x-1)e^x\right]=xe^x;\quad\left[(x-1)e^x\right]_0^1=0-(-1)=1\]
Why: \(\text{differentiate }x,\ \text{integrate }e^x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e-1=\displaystyle\int_0^1e^x\,dx\); (B) \(e=\left[xe^x\right]_0^1\); (D) \(0\ne1\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int xe^x\,dx=(x-1)e^x+C\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Integration: by parts and definite integrals

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Composition of a function with itself
questions.question: Let f(x)=(x−1)/(x+1) for x≠−1. For x≠0 and x≠−1, what is f(f(x))?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −1/x.
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1},\quad x\ne-1\)
Formula/Principle: \(f(f(x))=\dfrac{f(x)-1}{f(x)+1}\)
Step 1: \(f(x)-1=\dfrac{x-1-(x+1)}{x+1}=\dfrac{-2}{x+1}\)
Step 2: \(f(x)+1=\dfrac{x-1+(x+1)}{x+1}=\dfrac{2x}{x+1}\)
Worked derivation: \[f(f(x))=\frac{-2}{2x}=-\frac1x\]
Check: \[x=3:\ f(3)=\tfrac12,\ f\left(\tfrac12\right)=\frac{-1/2}{3/2}=-\tfrac13\]
Why: \(f(x)\ne-1\ \text{requires}\ x\ne0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x:\ f(f(3))=-\tfrac13\ne3\); (B) \(\tfrac1x:\ \tfrac13\ne-\tfrac13\); (C) \(-x:\ -3\ne-\tfrac13\).
Key point: \(\text{substitute the whole expression, then simplify}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A 3×3 determinant D has rows r₁,r₂,r₃. After replacing r₂ by r₂+3r₁ and interchanging r₁ with r₃, the result is −10. What is D?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10.
Given: \(D=\det(r_1,r_2,r_3);\quad r_2\to r_2+3r_1;\quad r_1\leftrightarrow r_3;\quad\text{result}=-10\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{adding a multiple of a row}:\ \det\ \text{unchanged};\quad\text{interchange}:\ \det\to-\det\)
Step 1: \(\det(r_1,\ r_2+3r_1,\ r_3)=D\)
Step 2: \(\det(r_3,\ r_2+3r_1,\ r_1)=-D\)
Worked derivation: \[-D=-10\Rightarrow D=10\]
Check: \[D=\det\operatorname{diag}(1,2,5)=10:\ \det\begin{pmatrix}0&0&5\\3&2&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}=-10\]
Why: \(\det\ \text{is linear in each row and alternating}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-30\) (factor 3 applied, sign kept); (B) \(-10\) (interchange ignored); (D) \(30\) (factor 3 applied).
Key point: \(R_i\to R_i+kR_j\ \text{leaves the determinant unchanged}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Bayes update from two conditionally independent tests
questions.question: In a hypothetical classification experiment, 10% of objects are type X. A test returns positive with probability 0.8 for X and 0.1 for non-X. Two repetitions are independent conditional on the object's type. An object tests positive first and negative second. What is the probability it is X?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 16/97.
Given: \(P(X)=0.1;\quad P(+|X)=0.8,\ P(+|\bar X)=0.1;\quad\text{tests independent given the type};\quad\text{result}\ (+,-)\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(X|+,-)=\dfrac{P(X)P(+,-|X)}{P(X)P(+,-|X)+P(\bar X)P(+,-|\bar X)}\)
Step 1: \(P(+,-|X)=0.8\times0.2=0.16\)
Step 2: \(P(+,-|\bar X)=0.1\times0.9=0.09\)
Step 3: \(P(X)P(+,-|X)=0.016,\quad P(\bar X)P(+,-|\bar X)=0.081\)
Worked derivation: \[P(X|+,-)=\frac{0.016}{0.016+0.081}=\frac{16}{97}\approx0.165\]
Check: \[\text{after }+:\ \frac{0.08}{0.17}=\frac{8}{17};\quad\text{after }-:\ \frac{\frac{8}{17}(0.2)}{\frac{8}{17}(0.2)+\frac{9}{17}(0.9)}=\frac{1.6}{9.7}\]
Why: \(\text{the negative result lowers the probability raised by the positive one}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{8}{17}\) (first test only); (C) \(\dfrac89=\dfrac{0.8}{0.9}\); (D) \(\dfrac1{10}\) (prior).
Key point: \(\text{posterior}\propto\text{prior}\times\text{likelihood of all the data}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Probability: conditional probability and Bayes theorem

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: In (x+2)⁶, what is the ratio of the coefficient of x³ to the coefficient of x⁴?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8/3.
Given: \((x+2)^6\)
Formula/Principle: \([x^r]\,(x+2)^6=\dbinom6r2^{6-r}\)
Step 1: \([x^3]=\dbinom63\cdot2^3=160\)
Step 2: \([x^4]=\dbinom64\cdot2^2=60\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{160}{60}=\frac83\]
Check: \[\frac{\binom63}{\binom64}\times2=\frac{20}{15}\times2=\frac83\]
Why: \(T_{r+1}=\dbinom6rx^r2^{6-r}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\) (binomial coefficients omitted); (B) \(\dfrac{20}{15}=\dfrac43\) (powers of 2 omitted); (C) \(3\ne\dfrac83\).
Key point: \(\text{the power of 2 is }6-r,\ \text{not }r\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Compare AP and GP sums with shared endpoints
questions.question: A geometric progression has first term 1 and common ratio 2. Its first n terms sum to 1023. An arithmetic progression has the same n, the same first term and the same last term as those GP terms. By how much does the AP sum exceed the GP sum?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1542.
Given: \(\text{GP}:\ a=1,\ r=2,\ S_n=1023;\quad\text{AP}:\ \text{same }n,\ \text{first and last terms}\)
Formula/Principle: \(S_n^{\text{GP}}=\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1},\quad S_n^{\text{AP}}=\dfrac n2(a+l)\)
Step 1: \(2^n-1=1023\Rightarrow n=10\)
Step 2: \(l=2^{9}=512\)
Step 3: \(S^{\text{AP}}=\dfrac{10}{2}(1+512)=2565\)
Worked derivation: \[2565-1023=1542\]
Check: \[1+2+4+\dots+512=1023\]
Why: \(\text{AP terms lie above GP terms between the common endpoints}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1023=S^{\text{GP}}\); (B) \(2565=S^{\text{AP}}\); (D) \(2046=2\times1023\).
Key point: \(\text{find }n\ \text{first}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Sequences and series: finite arithmetic and geometric sums

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=sin(kx)/x for nonzero x and f(0)=2. For which real k is f continuous at x=0?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2.
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{\sin kx}{x}\ (x\ne0),\quad f(0)=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin kx}{x}=k\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin kx}{kx}=k\)
Worked derivation: \[k=f(0)=2\]
Check: \[x=0.01:\ \frac{\sin0.02}{0.01}=1.9999\]
Why: \(\text{continuity}:\ \displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=f(0)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=-2:\ \lim=-2\ne2\); (B) \(k=0:\ \lim=0\); (C) \(k=1:\ \lim=1\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin kx}{x}=k\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Line perpendicular to a given line
questions.question: What is the equation of the line through (2,3) perpendicular to 3x+4y=5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4x−3y+1=0.
Given: \(P=(2,3),\quad L:\ 3x+4y=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(m_1m_2=-1\)
Step 1: \(m_L=-\dfrac34\Rightarrow m_\perp=\dfrac43\)
Step 2: \(y-3=\dfrac43(x-2)\Rightarrow3y-9=4x-8\)
Worked derivation: \[4x-3y+1=0\]
Check: \[4(2)-3(3)+1=0;\quad(3)(4)+(4)(-3)=0\]
Why: \(\text{line}\perp ax+by=c\ \text{has the form}\ bx-ay=k\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3x+4y-18=0\) (parallel to \(L\)); (C) \(4x+3y-17=0:\ (3)(4)+(4)(3)=24\ne0\); (D) \(3x-4y+6=0:\ (3)(3)+(4)(-4)=-7\ne0\).
Key point: \(a_1a_2+b_1b_2=0\ \text{for perpendicular lines}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A path from (0,0) to (4,4) uses only right and up steps. How many paths pass through exactly one of A=(1,2) and B=(3,2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 42.
Given: \((0,0)\to(4,4),\ \text{steps R, U};\quad A=(1,2),\ B=(3,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(N[(0,0)\to(p,q)]=\dbinom{p+q}{p};\quad N_{\text{exactly one}}=N_A+N_B-2N_{AB}\)
Step 1: \(N_A=\dbinom31\dbinom52=3\times10=30\)
Step 2: \(N_B=\dbinom53\dbinom31=10\times3=30\)
Step 3: \(N_{AB}=\dbinom31\cdot1\cdot\dbinom31=9\)
Worked derivation: \[30+30-2(9)=42\]
Check: \[\text{total}=\binom84=70\ge30+30-9=51\]
Why: \(\text{paths through both are counted in }N_A\text{ and in }N_B\)
Why not the others: (A) \(60\) (\(N_{AB}\) not removed); (C) \(51\) (at least one); (D) \(9=N_{AB}\).
Key point: \(\text{exactly one}=|A|+|B|-2|A\cap B|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A polynomial with real coefficients has 2+i as a root. Which statement must be true?
options: C) Its degree is exactly two
D) Its constant term is positive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2−i is also a root.
Given: \(p(x)\in\mathbb R[x],\quad p(2+i)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\overline{p(z)}=p(\bar z)\ \text{for real coefficients}\)
Step 1: \(p(2-i)=p(\overline{2+i})=\overline{p(2+i)}=\bar0\)
Worked derivation: \[p(2-i)=0\]
Check: \[(x-2-i)(x-2+i)=x^2-4x+5\in\mathbb R[x]\]
Why: \(\text{non-real roots of real polynomials occur in conjugate pairs}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x^2-4x+5\ \text{at}\ -2+i:\ 3-4i+8-4i+5\ne0\); (C) \((x-1)(x^2-4x+5)\ \text{has degree 3}\); (D) \(-(x^2-4x+5)\ \text{has constant term}\ -5\).
Key point: \(p(z)=0\Rightarrow p(\bar z)=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Initial-value solution and area after proving curve ordering
questions.question: For x>0, let \(y'=1+y/x\) and y(1)=0. What is the area between the solution curve and the line \(y=x-1\) over \(1\le x\le e\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((4e-e^2-1)/4\).
Given: \(y'=1+\dfrac yx,\quad x>0,\quad y(1)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\left(\dfrac yx\right)'=\dfrac{y'}{x}-\dfrac{y}{x^2}\)
Step 1: \(y'-\dfrac yx=1\Rightarrow\left(\dfrac yx\right)'=\dfrac1x\Rightarrow\dfrac yx=\ln x+C\)
Step 2: \(y(1)=0\Rightarrow C=0\Rightarrow y=x\ln x\)
Step 3: \(g(x)=x\ln x-(x-1):\ g(1)=0,\ g'(x)=\ln x\ge0\ (x\ge1)\Rightarrow x\ln x\ge x-1\)
Step 4: \(\displaystyle\int_1^ex\ln x\,dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x-\frac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^e=\frac{e^2}{4}+\frac14\)
Step 5: \(\displaystyle\int_1^e(x-1)\,dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-x\right]_1^e=\frac{e^2}{2}-e+\frac12\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{Area}=\frac{e^2+1}{4}-\frac{2e^2-4e+2}{4}=\frac{4e-e^2-1}{4}\approx0.62\]
Check: \[x=e:\ e\ln e=e>e-1\]
Why: \(\text{area}=\displaystyle\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac{e^2-1}{4}\ne\dfrac{e^2+1}{4}-\dfrac{(e-1)^2}{2}\); (C) \(\dfrac{e^2+1}{4}=\displaystyle\int_1^ex\ln x\,dx\) (line not subtracted); (D) \(e-1\ne0.62\).
Key point: \(\text{check which curve is on top before integrating}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Differential equations: homogeneous equation; integration: area

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: If sin θ+cos θ=1/2 for real θ, what is sin 2θ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −3/4.
Given: \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\dfrac12\)
Formula/Principle: \((\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2=1+\sin2\theta\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac14=1+\sin2\theta\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin2\theta=\frac14-1=-\frac34\]
Check: \[|\sin2\theta|=\tfrac34\le1\]
Why: \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\quad2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\)
Why not the others: (B) \(-\tfrac12\); (C) \(\tfrac14=(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2\); (D) \(+\tfrac34\) (sign).
Key point: \(\text{square the sum}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A displacement obeys x=At²+B sin(ωt), where x is length and t is time. What are dimensions of A and B, respectively?
options: A) L T⁻¹ and L T⁻²
D) L T⁻² and L T
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) L T⁻² and L.
Given: \(x=At^2+B\sin(\omega t),\quad[x]=\mathrm L,\ [t]=\mathrm T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{each term has the dimension of }x;\ \text{a sine is dimensionless}\)
Step 1: \([A]\,\mathrm T^2=\mathrm L\)
Step 2: \([B]\cdot1=\mathrm L\)
Worked derivation: \[[A]=\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}},\qquad[B]=\mathrm L\]
Check: \[[\omega t]=\mathrm{T^{-1}\cdot T}=1\]
Why: \(\text{only quantities of the same dimension can be added}\)
Why not the others: (A) \([A]=\mathrm{LT^{-1}}:\ [At^2]=\mathrm{LT}\ne\mathrm L\); (C) \([A]=\mathrm L:\ [At^2]=\mathrm{LT^2}\); (D) \([B]=\mathrm{LT}\ne\mathrm L\).
Key point: \(\text{principle of homogeneity}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two blocks of masses m and 2m are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. What is acceleration magnitude when released?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) g/3.
Given: \(m_1=m,\quad m_2=2m,\quad\text{light string, frictionless pulley}\)
Formula/Principle: \(2mg-T=2ma,\quad T-mg=ma\)
Step 1: \(\text{add}:\ mg=3ma\)
Worked derivation: \[a=\frac g3\]
Check: \[T=m(g+a)=\tfrac43mg;\quad2mg-\tfrac43mg=\tfrac23mg=2m\cdot\tfrac g3\]
Why: \(\text{the string makes both accelerations equal in magnitude}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac g2\) (driven mass \(m\), total \(2m\)); (B) \(\dfrac g4\); (D) \(\dfrac{2g}{3}\) (net force \(2mg\)).
Key point: \(a=\dfrac{m_2-m_1}{m_2+m_1}g\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two wires of equal material and length, with cross-sectional areas A and 2A, are connected in series and pulled by force F. What is extension of the narrower wire divided by extension of the wider one?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2.
Given: \(\text{same }Y,\ L;\quad A_1=A,\ A_2=2A;\quad\text{series, force }F\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta L=\dfrac{FL}{AY}\)
Step 1: \(\text{series}\Rightarrow\text{same }F\ \text{in both}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Delta L_1}{\Delta L_2}=\frac{A_2}{A_1}=2\]
Check: \[\text{stress}_1=\frac FA=2\times\frac{F}{2A}\]
Why: \(\text{same force, smaller area}\Rightarrow\text{larger stress and strain}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12\) (inverted); (B) \(1\) (area ignored); (C) \(4\) (\(\Delta L\propto A^{-2}\)).
Key point: \(\Delta L\propto\dfrac{1}{A}\ \text{at fixed }F,\ L,\ Y\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A metal rod fits exactly between two rigid supports at 20°C. Temperature rises by ΔT while supports stay fixed and the rod remains elastic. What is the magnitude of compressive stress, if its Young modulus is Y and expansion coefficient α?
options: D) Zero because length is fixed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) YαΔT.
Given: \(\text{rod between rigid supports},\ \Delta T,\ Y,\ \alpha\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{free expansion strain}=\alpha\,\Delta T;\quad\sigma=Y\times\text{strain}\)
Step 1: \(\text{supports prevent expansion}\Rightarrow\text{compressive strain}=\alpha\,\Delta T\)
Worked derivation: \[\sigma=Y\alpha\,\Delta T\]
Check: \[\text{steel}:\ 2\times10^{11}\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times10=2.4\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa}\]
Why: \(\text{the supports must undo the thermal expansion elastically}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\left[\dfrac{Y\Delta T}{\alpha}\right]=\mathrm{Pa\,K^2}\); (C) \(\left[\dfrac{\alpha\Delta T}{Y}\right]=\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}\); (D) \(\text{fixed length}\Rightarrow\text{strain}\ne0\ \text{relative to the free length}\).
Key point: \(\text{thermal stress}=Y\alpha\,\Delta T\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A diatomic ideal gas has rotations active but vibrations frozen in the listed temperature range. If its measured molar CV is near 5R/2, what is expected molar CP?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7R/2.
Given: \(C_V=\dfrac52R\)
Formula/Principle: \(C_P-C_V=R\)
Step 1: \(f=3+2=5\Rightarrow C_V=\dfrac f2R=\dfrac52R\)
Worked derivation: \[C_P=\frac52R+R=\frac72R\]
Check: \[\gamma=\frac{C_P}{C_V}=\frac75=1.4\]
Why: \(\text{Mayer's relation for an ideal gas}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac32R=C_V-R\); (C) \(\tfrac52R=C_V\); (D) \(\tfrac92R\) (vibration included).
Key point: \(C_P=C_V+R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: At a point on a circular path with constant speed, velocity points east. Which direction does acceleration point if the centre is north of that point?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) North.
Given: \(\text{uniform circular motion},\ \mathbf v\ \text{east},\ \text{centre north of the particle}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf a=-\dfrac{v^2}{r}\hat{\mathbf r}\ \ (\text{towards the centre})\)
Step 1: \(|\mathbf v|=\text{constant}\Rightarrow a_{\text{tangential}}=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf a=\frac{v^2}{r}\ \text{towards the centre}=\text{north}\]
Check: \[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v=0\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=0\]
Why: \(\text{only the direction of }\mathbf v\ \text{changes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\mathbf a\parallel\mathbf v\Rightarrow\text{speed increases}\); (B) \(\mathbf a\ \text{antiparallel to}\ \mathbf v\Rightarrow\text{speed decreases}\); (D) \(\mathbf a=0\Rightarrow\text{straight line}\).
Key point: \(\text{centripetal acceleration}=\dfrac{v^2}{r}\ \text{towards the centre}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Resonant frequencies of a closed pipe
questions.question: An air column in a pipe closed at one end is 0.85 m long. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What are its two lowest resonant frequencies?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 100 Hz and 300 Hz.
Given: \(L=0.85\ \mathrm m,\quad v=340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad\text{closed at one end}\)
Formula/Principle: \(f_n=\dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L},\ n=1,2,\dots\)
Step 1: \(f_1=\dfrac{340}{4\times0.85}=100\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Worked derivation: \[f_2=3f_1=300\ \mathrm{Hz}\]
Check: \[\lambda_1=4L=3.4\ \mathrm m;\quad\lambda_2=\frac{4L}{3}=1.13\ \mathrm m\]
Why: \(\text{node at the closed end, antinode at the open end}\Rightarrow L=(2n-1)\dfrac\lambda4\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{v}{2L}=200\ \mathrm{Hz},\ 400\ \mathrm{Hz}\) (open pipe); (B) \(200\ \mathrm{Hz}=2f_1\) (even harmonic absent); (C) \(200\ \mathrm{Hz}\ne\dfrac{v}{4L}\).
Key point: \(\text{closed pipe: odd harmonics only}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: A closed spherical Gaussian surface encloses +q and −3q; a +5q charge sits just outside it. What is the total electric flux through the sphere?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −2q/ε₀.
Given: \(\text{inside}:\ +q,\ -3q;\quad\text{outside}:\ +5q\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Phi=\dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(q_{\text{enclosed}}=q-3q=-2q\)
Worked derivation: \[\Phi=-\frac{2q}{\varepsilon_0}\]
Check: \[\text{field lines of }+5q\ \text{enter and leave}\Rightarrow\text{net flux }0\]
Why: \(\text{only enclosed charge contributes to the net flux}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(q-3q+5q=+3q\) (outside charge included); (C) \(+5q\) (outside charge only); (D) \(-3q\) (\(+q\) omitted).
Key point: \(\text{Gauss's law}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A network has R between A and B, another R between B and C, and a direct resistor 2R from A to C. Ideal wires make B a distinct node. What is equivalent resistance between A and C?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) R.
Given: \(R_{AB}=R,\ R_{BC}=R,\ R_{AC}=2R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{series}:\ R_1+R_2;\quad\text{parallel}:\ \dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}\)
Step 1: \(A\to B\to C:\ R+R=2R\)
Step 2: \(2R\parallel2R\)
Worked derivation: \[R_{AC}=\frac{2R\cdot2R}{4R}=R\]
Check: \[\text{equal branches}\Rightarrow\text{half of }2R\]
Why: \(B\ \text{carries no external connection}\Rightarrow AB,\ BC\ \text{in series}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac R2\) (\(R\parallel R\)); (C) \(2R\) (one branch only); (D) \(4R\) (all in series).
Key point: \(\text{reduce series groups first, then parallel}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A circular loop is viewed face-on. A magnetic field into the page increases in magnitude. Which direction is induced conventional current?
options: D) No induced current because field direction stays fixed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Counterclockwise, producing outward field.
Given: \(\mathbf B\ \text{into the page},\ |\mathbf B|\ \text{increasing}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\ \ (\text{Lenz's law})\)
Step 1: \(\text{inward flux increasing}\Rightarrow\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}\ \text{out of the page}\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}\ \text{out of the page}\Rightarrow\text{current counterclockwise (right-hand rule)}\]
Check: \[\text{clockwise current}\Rightarrow\mathbf B\ \text{inward}\Rightarrow\text{flux grows faster (energy not conserved)}\]
Why: \(\text{the induced current opposes the change in flux}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{reinforcing the change violates Lenz's law}\); (C) \(\text{clockwise current gives an inward field}\); (D) \(\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{oppose the change, not the field}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Resonant angular frequency of a series LCR circuit
questions.question: A series LCR circuit has L = 0.10 H, C = 10 μF and R = 20 Ω. At what angular frequency of the source is the current amplitude greatest?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1000 rad s⁻¹.
Given: \(L=0.10\ \mathrm H,\quad C=10\ \mu\mathrm F=1.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm F,\quad R=20\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_0=\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2+\left(\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2}};\quad\text{maximum at}\ \omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\)
Step 1: \(LC=0.10\times1.0\times10^{-5}=1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-6}}}=1000\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[X_L=\omega_0L=100\ \Omega;\quad X_C=\frac{1}{\omega_0C}=100\ \Omega\]
Why: \(X_L=X_C\Rightarrow Z=R\ (\text{minimum})\)
Why not the others: (A) \(100:\ X_L=10\ \Omega,\ X_C=1000\ \Omega\); (B) \(500:\ X_L=50\ \Omega,\ X_C=200\ \Omega\); (D) \(10^4:\ X_L=1000\ \Omega,\ X_C=10\ \Omega\).
Key point: \(\omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\ \text{does not depend on }R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image of an object 30 cm in front of it. A plane mirror is placed exactly at the image plane, perpendicular to the axis. Where do returned rays form the final image after passing back through the lens?
options: B) 30 cm on the object side
C) 20 cm on the object side
D) 60 cm on the mirror side
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 30 cm on the object side.
Given: \(f=+20\ \mathrm{cm},\quad u=-30\ \mathrm{cm};\quad\text{plane mirror at the image plane}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac1{20}-\dfrac1{30}=\dfrac1{60}\Rightarrow v=60\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\text{mirror at the image}\Rightarrow\text{image in the mirror coincides with it (object distance 0)}\)
Step 3: \(\text{return pass}:\ \text{object 60 cm from the lens}\Rightarrow\dfrac1{v'}=\dfrac1{20}-\dfrac1{60}=\dfrac1{30}\)
Worked derivation: \[v'=30\ \mathrm{cm}\ \text{on the object side}\]
Check: \[m=\left(-\tfrac{60}{30}\right)\left(-\tfrac{30}{60}\right)=+1\ \ (\text{final image coincides with the object})\]
Why: \(\text{object and image positions of a lens are interchangeable}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(v'=0\ne30\ \mathrm{cm}\); (C) \(20\ \mathrm{cm}=f\) (needs the object at infinity); (D) \(60\ \mathrm{cm}\) (first image, before reflection).
Key point: \(\text{conjugate points}:\ u\leftrightarrow v\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Infer amplitudes from contrast then apply intensity attenuation
questions.question: Two coherent beams interfere with \(I_{\max}/I_{\min}=9\). The weaker beam's intensity is then reduced to one quarter of its original value, with coherence maintained. What is the new visibility \((I_{\max}-I_{\min})/(I_{\max}+I_{\min})\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8/17.
Given: \(\dfrac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}}=9;\quad I_2\to\dfrac{I_2}{4}\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_{\max}=(a_1+a_2)^2,\quad I_{\min}=(a_1-a_2)^2,\quad I\propto a^2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}=3\Rightarrow a_1=2a_2\)
Step 2: \(I_2\to\dfrac{I_2}{4}\Rightarrow a_2'=\dfrac{a_2}{2}\Rightarrow a_1=4a_2'\)
Step 3: \(I_{\max}'=(5a_2')^2=25a_2'^2,\quad I_{\min}'=(3a_2')^2=9a_2'^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{I_{\max}'-I_{\min}'}{I_{\max}'+I_{\min}'}=\frac{25-9}{25+9}=\frac{16}{34}=\frac{8}{17}\]
Check: \[\frac{2\sqrt{I_1I_2'}}{I_1+I_2'}=\frac{2\sqrt{16\cdot1}}{16+1}=\frac{8}{17}\]
Why: \(\text{amplitudes add, intensities do not}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac45\) (visibility before the change); (B) \(\dfrac12\); (C) \(\dfrac14\) (intensity ratio taken as the answer).
Key point: \(\text{visibility}=\dfrac{2a_1a_2}{a_1^2+a_2^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron and a proton each start from rest and are accelerated through the same potential difference V. What is the ratio of their nonrelativistic de Broglie wavelengths λe/λp?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) √(mp/me).
Given: \(\text{same }|q|=e,\ \text{same }V,\ \text{from rest}\)
Formula/Principle: \(K=eV=\dfrac{p^2}{2m},\quad\lambda=\dfrac hp\)
Step 1: \(p=\sqrt{2meV}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt m}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}=\sqrt{\frac{m_p}{m_e}}\approx\sqrt{1836}\approx43\]
Check: \[m_e<m_p\Rightarrow p_e<p_p\Rightarrow\lambda_e>\lambda_p\]
Why: \(\text{equal kinetic energy, unequal momentum}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\sqrt{\dfrac{m_e}{m_p}}\) (inverted); (C) \(\dfrac{m_p}{m_e}\) (equal speeds assumed); (D) \(1\) (equal momenta assumed).
Key point: \(\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The diode I–V plot has nearly zero forward current up to about 0.6 V, then a sharp rise; reverse current remains small until a large negative voltage. Which operating point best corresponds to ordinary forward conduction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +0.8 V, large positive current.
Given: \(\text{forward}:\ I\approx0\ \text{for}\ V<0.6\ \mathrm V,\ \text{then a sharp rise};\quad\text{reverse}:\ I\ \text{small until breakdown}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{forward conduction requires}\ V>V_{\text{threshold}}\approx0.6\ \mathrm V\)
Step 1: \(+0.8\ \mathrm V>0.6\ \mathrm V\)
Worked derivation: \[V=+0.8\ \mathrm V\Rightarrow I\ \text{large and positive}\]
Check: \[+0.2\ \mathrm V<0.6\ \mathrm V\Rightarrow I\approx0\]
Why: \(\text{the applied forward voltage must overcome the barrier potential}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(V<0\Rightarrow I\approx-I_{\text{sat}}\ (\text{small})\); (B) \(0.2\ \mathrm V<0.6\ \mathrm V\Rightarrow I\approx0\); (C) \(|{-0.8}\ \mathrm V|\ll V_{\text{breakdown}}\Rightarrow I\ \text{small}\).
Key point: \(\text{silicon diode: knee voltage about }0.6\text{–}0.7\ \mathrm V\)
